items.title: [AI Feed Curator] State of the Feed — Week of October 12–18, 2026
items.content_html:
Week of October 12–18, 2026: The feed ran 7 times this week, fetching an average of 1,359 articles per run and delivering an average of 81 quality articles per run. Category volume was led by ai-tech (126 articles), followed by news (98), wellness (70), science (56), climate (51), local (50), design (42), homelab (33), outdoors (16), homestead (14), and scifi (12). Scoring used the dimensional Q/R/L composite model (quality, relevance, local) with weights of 0.25, 0.55, and 0.20 respectively.

Pipeline efficiency averaged 2.36 articles fetched per article delivered over 14 runs, with a range of 0.96 to 3.28. The ratio sits in the middle of its observed range, indicating moderate filtering overhead rather than an unusually high noise load. The new feed blog.hmvh.net was added this week. Four feeds reported errors during the period: Hacker News, EEVblog, Singularity Hub, and NRDC.

Feed discovery surfaced several candidates, led by Meshtastic Blog (score 85.9), followed by My Cariboo Now, Cariboo News, Events, Weather and Local Radio (each scored 72.3).

items.content_html:
Amid blackouts, artillery fire and the onslaught of Russian drone attacks, the Richelievsky in Kherson provides a refuge for those with nowhere else to go

There is one important rule in the Richelievsky, Kherson’s last functioning hotel: close the curtains before dusk. Less than a kilometre away lies the Dnipro, the river that has formed the frontline since Ukrainian forces liberated Kherson in November 2022; Moscow’s troops are on the opposite bank.

In a city where Russian drone operators hunt civilians in what is now widely known as the “human safari”, even a sliver of light escaping through a window may be enough to reveal someone’s location after dark.

Hotel manager Yevhen Emtsov, 46, in the building’s former conference room

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.

Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

Amini, an accounting student, is being held in Vakilabad prison in the north-east city of Mashhad. She has been sentenced to more than 12 years in prison and death in separate cases heard by a revolutionary and a criminal court.
